questions.topic: Why the tertiary sector has grown to dominate the Indian economy
questions.question: Over the forty years between 1973-74 and 2013-14, production in all three sectors of the Indian economy increased, but it increased the most in the tertiary sector, which by 2013-14 had emerged as India's largest producing sector, replacing the primary sector. Why do you think the tertiary sector has become so popular in India? Give three reasons.

rubric.point: Basic services (hospitals, education, postal services, police, courts, administration, defence, transport, banks, insurance) are needed in any country, and in a developing country the government has to take responsibility for providing many of these

The development of agriculture and industry itself generates demand for supporting services (transport, trade, storage) - the more the primary and secondary sectors grow, the more such services are needed

As income levels rise, people demand more services such as eating out, tourism, shopping, private hospitals/schools and professional training; additionally, new technology-based services (based on ICT) have become important and are growing rapidly in recent decades

questions.model_answer: The tertiary sector has grown to dominate the Indian economy for several reasons. First, every country needs a range of basic services - hospitals, schools, postal and police services, courts, administration, defence, transport, banking and insurance - and in a developing country like India, government has had to take primary responsibility for providing many of these. Second, the growth of agriculture and industry itself creates demand for supporting services like transport, trade and storage - so as the primary and secondary sectors expand, so does the need for tertiary-sector support. Third, as income levels rise, people increasingly demand additional services such as eating out, tourism, private healthcare and education, and professional training; more recently, entirely new technology-based services relying on information and communication technology have become essential and have been growing especially rapidly, further boosting the tertiary sector's share of the economy.

questions.topic: Disguised unemployment in agriculture and its solutions
questions.question: Mr Y, visiting a rural area from a city, finds five people working on a small agricultural farm where more than two people are not actually required - removing the other three would not affect production. How can this problem of underemployment in rural areas be solved?

rubric.point: The surplus workers should take up different jobs to raise total family income - e.g. employment in building dams, canals or roads in the village

Government investment in transportation/storage of crops and better rural roads can help create alternative opportunities, and promoting agro-based industries (dal mills, cold storage) lets farmers store and sell produce (like potatoes/onions) when prices are favourable, generating income

Setting up honey collection centres or vegetable/produce processing industries near forest/farm areas, and government loans at lower interest rates for rural entrepreneurship, can also create alternative employment and reduce disguised unemployment

questions.model_answer: The three surplus workers on the farm should ideally shift into different kinds of work that raise the family's total income rather than remaining under-employed in agriculture - for example, they could be employed in building dams, canals or roads in the village. More broadly, the problem can be tackled through government investment in transportation and storage of crops and better rural roads (so produce can reach markets efficiently), and by promoting agro-based industries like dal mills or cold storage facilities, which let farmers store crops such as potatoes and onions and sell them when prices are more favourable. Setting up honey collection centres in forest-adjacent villages, establishing produce-processing industries, and providing government loans at lower interest rates to support new rural enterprises can all create the additional employment needed to absorb workers who are currently underemployed in agriculture.

questions.topic: Comparing the organised and unorganised sectors through a real scenario
questions.question: Sunil and Raman graduated from the same college. Sunil was employed in the unorganised sector and was unhappy, while Raman was employed in the organised sector and was happy. Explain why, giving three points of difference between the two sectors.

rubric.point: In the organised sector, workers enjoy security of employment, fixed working hours (with overtime pay if they work more), and benefits like paid leave, provident fund, gratuity and medical benefits, plus legally mandated safe working conditions - explaining Raman's satisfaction

The unorganised sector is characterised by small, scattered units largely outside government control; rules exist but often aren't followed, jobs are low-paid and often irregular, with no overtime, paid leave or job security - workers can be let go without reason - explaining Sunil's dissatisfaction

questions.model_answer: Raman, in the organised sector, was happy because such jobs come with security of employment, a fixed number of working hours (with mandatory overtime pay if he works more), and additional benefits like paid leave, payment during holidays, provident fund, gratuity and medical benefits - with the law also requiring the employer to ensure basic facilities like drinking water and a safe working environment, plus a pension on retirement. Sunil, in the unorganised sector, was unhappy because that sector is characterised by small, scattered units that are largely outside government control; while rules and regulations exist, they are often not followed in practice - jobs tend to be low-paid, irregular, and insecure, with no provision for overtime, paid leave, or sick leave, and workers can be dismissed without reason, especially during slow seasons.

questions.question: Which of the following comes under the secondary sector of the economy?
questions.explanation: The secondary sector covers activities that transform natural/raw products into other forms through manufacturing - a basket weaver transforms raw material (like cane or bamboo) into a finished product, so this is a secondary-sector activity. Bee-keeping and fishing extract products directly from nature (primary sector), while money-lending is a service (tertiary sector).
questions.subject: economics

questions.question: Natural products being changed into other forms through a manufacturing process is known as producing a:
questions.explanation: When natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing, it is a secondary-sector activity and what is produced is a secondary product - for example, cotton (a primary product) manufactured into cloth.

questions.question: Analyse the role of the tertiary sector in the Indian economy.

rubric.point: the tertiary sector (services) does not produce a good itself but helps in the production process, including transport, storage, communication, banking and trade
today the tertiary sector produces the largest share of India's GDP and employs large numbers of people, including both basic services and fast-growing modern services like IT and banking

questions.model_answer: The tertiary sector, or the service sector, does not produce a good itself but helps in the production process through activities like transport, storage, communication, banking and trade. Today it produces the largest share of India's Gross Domestic Product and employs a growing number of people, ranging from basic services like education, hospitals and public administration to fast-growing modern services such as information technology, banking and tourism.

questions.question: Differentiate between primary and secondary sectors with examples.

rubric.point: the primary sector covers activities that directly exploit/use natural resources, such as agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry and mining
the secondary sector covers activities that manufacture/transform natural products through an industrial process, such as cotton into cloth or sugarcane into sugar
the secondary sector is also known as the industrial sector, and is gradually associated with a rise in value addition over the raw materials used by the primary sector

questions.model_answer: The primary sector covers activities that directly exploit or use natural resources, such as agriculture, dairy farming, fishing, forestry and mining. The secondary sector, also called the industrial sector, covers activities that manufacture or transform these natural products through an industrial process into a different, more valuable form - for example, cotton (a primary product) is manufactured into cloth, and sugarcane is processed into sugar, in both cases adding value over the raw material.

questions.topic: Tertiary sector and rural job creation
questions.question: Assess the potential for job creation through the expansion of the tertiary sector in rural areas.

rubric.point: growth of services like transport, storage of agricultural produce, trade/marketing of farm goods and rural banking/credit can create new employment outside farming
new services such as agro-processing, cold storage and tourism can also be started in villages to absorb surplus agricultural labour
this can help reduce disguised unemployment/underemployment that is common in agriculture in rural India

questions.model_answer: Expanding tertiary-sector services in rural areas - such as transport and storage of agricultural produce, trade and marketing of farm goods, veterinary services, and rural banking and credit institutions - can create substantial new employment outside farming itself. New activities like agro-processing, cold storage facilities, rural tourism and IT-enabled services could also be developed to absorb surplus agricultural labour. This has significant potential to reduce the disguised unemployment and underemployment that is common among people dependent on agriculture in rural India, since farms often carry more workers than they actually need.
